title: Gaussian Mixture Models Quiz
description: Test your understanding of gaussian mixture models

questions.question: What is the main difference between hard clustering (like K-Means) and soft clustering (like GMM)?
options: Hard clustering is faster than soft clustering
Hard clustering assigns each point to exactly one cluster, while soft clustering provides probabilistic assignments
Hard clustering works better with overlapping clusters
Hard clustering requires fewer parameters
questions.explanation: The key difference is that hard clustering assigns each point to exactly one cluster (binary assignment), while soft clustering provides probabilistic assignments where each point has a probability of belonging to each cluster.

questions.question: In the EM algorithm for GMM, what does the E-step calculate?
options: The component parameters (means, covariances, weights)
The responsibilities (posterior probabilities) of each point for each component
The log-likelihood of the data
The number of components needed
questions.explanation: The E-step (Expectation step) calculates the responsibilities γᵢₖ, which are the posterior probabilities that each point xᵢ belongs to each component k, given the current parameter estimates.

questions.question: What does the M-step in the EM algorithm do?
options: Calculates the responsibilities for each data point
Updates the component parameters (means, covariances, weights) to maximize likelihood
Determines the optimal number of components
Initializes the algorithm parameters
questions.explanation: The M-step (Maximization step) updates the component parameters (means, covariances, and mixing weights) to maximize the likelihood of the data given the current responsibilities calculated in the E-step.

questions.question: Which covariance type allows clusters to have any shape and orientation?
options: Diagonal covariance
Spherical covariance
Full covariance
Tied covariance
questions.explanation: Full covariance allows the covariance matrix to have any values, enabling clusters to be elliptical with any orientation and shape. Diagonal restricts to axis-aligned ellipses, and spherical restricts to circles.

questions.question: For model selection in GMM, what do AIC and BIC help determine?
options: The best initialization method
The optimal number of components (K)
The convergence tolerance
The covariance type to use
questions.explanation: AIC (Akaike Information Criterion) and BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion) are information criteria used to select the optimal number of components K by balancing model fit with model complexity.

questions.question: Which statement about BIC vs AIC is correct?
options: BIC is less conservative and tends to select more complex models
AIC is more conservative and tends to select simpler models
BIC is more conservative and tends to select simpler models
BIC and AIC always give the same result
questions.explanation: BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion) is more conservative than AIC and tends to select simpler models with fewer components, especially as the dataset size increases, due to its stronger penalty for model complexity.

questions.question: What is a 'responsibility' in the context of GMM?
options: The weight of each component in the mixture
The probability that a data point belongs to a specific component
The covariance matrix of a component
The mean of a component
questions.explanation: A responsibility γᵢₖ is the posterior probability that data point xᵢ belongs to component k. It represents the 'soft assignment' of points to clusters in probabilistic clustering.

questions.question: Why might GMM be preferred over K-Means for certain datasets?
options: GMM is always faster than K-Means
GMM can handle overlapping clusters and provides uncertainty estimates
GMM requires fewer parameters than K-Means
GMM works better with spherical clusters
questions.explanation: GMM is preferred when you have overlapping clusters, need uncertainty estimates for cluster assignments, want non-spherical cluster shapes, or need a probabilistic model. K-Means assumes spherical, well-separated clusters.
